the-kentucky-raid-of-1847.t: The raiders’ own home paper, the Covington Licking Valley Register of 17 September 1847, put their bail at “something over four thousand dollars.” Every later account we have found gives $2,600, the 1882 county history’s figure.
the-kentucky-raid-of-1847.s: The county histories of 1875, 1882 and 1906; the House Divided project’s narrative of the 1847 stampedes; D. G. Chardavoyne’s article in The Court Legacy (2004); Wikipedia; the Underground Railroad Society of Cass County’s pages; the Clio entry; the State Bar of Michigan’s milestone pages; web searches for the bail figure.

the-kentucky-raid-of-1847.t: The same 1847 Kentucky account says the raiders’ baggage wagon, its wheels taken, “was then delivered up.” The earliest telling we know of the story that it was rolled into Birch Lake is in newspapers of 1936–37, and no account we have found sets the two side by side.
the-kentucky-raid-of-1847.s: The county histories of 1875 and 1882, searched for “wagon”; the House Divided narrative; Wikipedia; the society’s pages; web searches for the wagon and Birch Lake.

the-bonine-house.t: The earliest description we have found of the building now called the Bonine carriage house: in 1882, “exactly opposite his residence, which is on a corner,” “the finely-built storehouse,” with two rows of arbor vitae running from it. The history says nothing of fugitives there.
the-bonine-house.s: The Underground Railroad Society of Cass County’s pages on the house and carriage house; eight Leader articles of 2009–2021; the Clio entries; local radio and television features; Wikipedia; web searches for Bonine with “storehouse” and “arbor vitae”.
the-bonine-house.alt: The 1882 county history on the Bonine farm
the-bonine-house.cap: History of Cass County (1882), p. 251. Internet Archive.

the-bonine-house.t: The Bonine named in Wilbur Siebert’s national directory of Underground Railroad workers (1898) is Isaac, the father: “Bogue, Steven. Bonine, Isaac. Shugart, Zachariah.” Modern accounts credit his son James E., and none we have found cites Siebert.
the-bonine-house.s: The same sources as for the storehouse, with web searches for Siebert with “Isaac Bonine”.
the-bonine-house.alt: Siebert 1898: Cass County, Bogue, Steven. Bonine, Isaac. Shugart, Zachariah.
the-bonine-house.cap: Siebert, The Underground Railroad (1898), Appendix E. Internet Archive.

the-bonine-house.t: Glover’s history of 1906 places the meeting of the Anti-Slavery Friends of Cass County, with the Rev. Charles Osborn as pastor, “in a log building in the grove on the farm of the late James E. Bonine … known as the Elk Park.” Modern accounts say only that the Bonines were members.
the-bonine-house.s: The same sources as for the storehouse, with web searches for the Anti-Slavery Friends with Bonine and Elk Park.
the-bonine-house.alt: Glover 1906 on the Anti-Slavery Friends at the Elk Park
the-bonine-house.cap: Glover, Twentieth Century History of Cass County (1906), p. 386. Internet Archive.

the-bonine-house.t: The earliest eyewitness account of the Bonine elk park, in the Michigan Farmer of 18 August 1885, says two elk “went to Victor Emanual, the King of Italy, … to grace the Royal Park,” with no warship, against the seven elk and “war vessel” of the 1882 county history. The same visitor describes a 40-acre park behind a ten-foot fence, ten elk and thirteen deer, the elk coming to the call “Come Bill!”, and a large fountain and flagstone walks before the house.
the-bonine-house.s: The Underground Railroad Society of Cass County’s pages on the house, carriage house and Quaker timeline; eight Leader articles of 2009–2021; the Clio entry; local radio and television features; Wikipedia; Internet Archive full-text searches for Bonine with elk, Italy and “Victor Emmanuel”; Italian sources on the wapiti of La Mandria, none of which names Michigan.
the-bonine-house.alt: Michigan Farmer 1885: two went to Victor Emanual, the King of Italy, to grace the Royal Park

the-bonine-house.t: The Bonine Elk Park outlived its founder by half a century. Isaac A. Bonine wrote to the federal Biological Survey in 1907 that he had bred elk “for about thirty-five years”; a 1908 newspaper reports elk sold at $100 a head to parks in Detroit and Grand Rapids; the WPA’s 1941 guide to Michigan found “more than a score of American elk” there, sold “to zoos, parks, and private gardens, and sometimes to Elk lodges”; and in October 1953 a newspaper photograph shows 12 to 15 elk still on the park. That was the year the farm left the family: G. Elwood Bonine’s 1976 obituary says the Elk Park Farms were in the family “from 1837 to 1953.”
the-bonine-house.s: The Underground Railroad Society of Cass County’s pages on the house, carriage house and Quaker timeline; eight Leader articles of 2009–2021; the Clio entries; local radio and television features; Wikipedia; Internet Archive full-text searches for “Bonine Elk Park” and “Elk Park farm”; the Biological Survey bulletins; the WPA guide; the Friends of Silverbrook obituary transcriptions.
the-bonine-house.card: East Jordan News-Herald|“A herd of 12 to 15 elk”|8 October 1953

the-bonine-house.t: The dates missing from modern accounts of the Bonines: James E. Bonine was born in Wayne County, Indiana, on 5 September 1816 and married Sarah Ann Bogue at Cassopolis on 8 August 1844; she was born in Preble County, Ohio, on 30 April 1825 and died at Vandalia on 17 September 1909. The Pioneer Society roll printed in 1906 gives James E. as coming to the county in 1841, a year before his father, not in 1843.
the-bonine-house.s: The Underground Railroad Society of Cass County’s pages on the house, carriage house and Quaker timeline; eight Leader articles of 2009–2021; the Clio entry; local radio and television features; Wikipedia; the Sharpless (1887), Bogue (1944) and Hannum (1911) genealogies; Indiana Quaker meeting abstracts; Glover’s 1906 history, p. 352, checked against the page image.

the-bonine-house.t: James E. Bonine was superintendent of the Air Line railroad through Penn Township, giving “three years time, $6,000 right of way, and $6,000 cash,” by the 1882 county history. The line was the Michigan Air Line, opened through Vandalia in 1871. No modern account of the Bonine House we have read mentions it.
the-bonine-house.s: The Underground Railroad Society of Cass County’s pages on the house, carriage house and Quaker timeline; eight Leader articles of 2009–2021; the Clio entry; local radio and television features; Wikipedia; web searches for Bonine with “Air Line” and railroad.

the-bonine-house.t: James E. Bonine, the builder of the Bonine House, died at his home in Niles on 18 February 1897, “in the eighty-first year of his age,” after an illness of four months, by his obituary in the Quaker weekly The American Friend. It says he built “principally one house for worship” and helped build three others. No modern account we have read gives the date; a 1906 Berrien County history gives 1898.
the-bonine-house.s: The Underground Railroad Society of Cass County’s pages on the house, carriage house and Quaker timeline; eight Leader articles of 2009–2021; the Clio entries; local radio and television features; Wikipedia; Find a Grave (a bot check stopped us) and Geni (a title only); Internet Archive full-text searches for James E. Bonine with died, funeral and 1897; the Friends of Silverbrook obituaries; Glover’s necrology.
the-bonine-house.alt: The American Friend 1897: Died at his home in Niles, Michigan, Second month 18th, 1897, James E. Bonine
the-bonine-house.cap: The American Friend, vol. 4 (1897), p. 308. Internet Archive.

the-bonine-house.t: The Italian side of the Bonine elk story has a record of its own. In 1871 the naturalist of the King of Italy’s park of La Mandria reported that the king had sent the Count di Castiglione “to America to buy wapiti,” that the first shipment of 60 landed 47 alive, and that the American elk kept dying through 1873. No account of the Bonine sale we have read connects it with the king’s buying in America.
the-bonine-house.s: The Underground Railroad Society of Cass County’s pages on the house, carriage house and Quaker timeline; eight Leader articles of 2009–2021; the Clio entries; local radio and television features; Wikipedia; Italian accounts of La Mandria (Rivista Savej, Fondazione 1563, Wikipedia); Internet Archive full-text searches for wapiti with Mandria and Castiglione.
the-bonine-house.alt: Comba 1871: the comte de Castiglione was sent by His Majesty to America to buy wapiti; 60 animals, 47 arrived alive in Italy
the-bonine-house.cap: Bulletin de la Société d’acclimatation (Paris, 1871), p. 500. Internet Archive.

_about: New findings, by story slug. Merged into each story's 'finds' by build_news.py and build_discoveries.py. Each: id, t (the finding, html), s (what we searched, html), town (filter label), img, alt, cap. Only findings checked as not previously published go here. Optional kind: New record, Earliest record, Correction, Connection, Identification, Map reading, Compilation or Myth tested.

e-clampus-vitus-the-complete-record.t: The earliest dated mention of E Clampus Vitus yet found anywhere: a letter from Connersville, Indiana, printed in the Indiana American of Brookville on 27 February 1846, which speaks of “the ‘Eclampsus Vitus’ society, an order of which, we have in our town.” The order’s own histories give no dated record before 1847.
e-clampus-vitus-the-complete-record.s: Full-text searches for “Eclampsus Vitus”, “Eclampses Vitus” and “Clampus Vitus”; Hoosier State Chronicles; Internet Archive; Wikipedia’s articles on E Clampus Vitus and Ephraim Bee and their references; ecvinc.org and chapter websites; Then and Now (E Clampus Vitus, 1966); the Shumate list of early lodges as given by the Julia C. Bulette chapter; HMDB; the 1888 Biographical and Historical Record of Vermillion County, Indiana, which dates the order there to about 1873.
e-clampus-vitus-the-complete-record.alt: A column of the Indiana American, 27 February 1846: our citizens are universally of the opinion that they are naturally qualified members of the Eclampsus Vitus society, an order of which we have in our town
e-clampus-vitus-the-complete-record.cap: Indiana American, Brookville, 27 Feb. 1846. Hoosier State Chronicles.

e-clampus-vitus-the-complete-record.t: An Indianapolis lodge in July 1846: the Indiana State Sentinel notified “the members of Tent No. 43 of the order of Eclampees Vitus” to meet in their hall on 16 July, “attired in full regalia.” No history of the order mentions Indiana.
e-clampus-vitus-the-complete-record.s: The searches listed for the Connersville letter, with web searches for the Sentinel and “Clampus”, and the Indiana State Library’s newspaper pages.
e-clampus-vitus-the-complete-record.alt: A notice in the Indiana State Sentinel, July 1846: the members of Tent No. 43 of the order of Eclampees Vitus are notified to meet in their Hall on Thursday evening, July 16, attired in full regalia
e-clampus-vitus-the-complete-record.cap: Indiana State Sentinel, Indianapolis, 16 July 1846. Hoosier State Chronicles.

e-clampus-vitus-the-complete-record.t: A lodge that asked a state legislature for a charter: House bill No. 242 in the Indiana House of Representatives, winter 1846–47, “to incorporate Jackson Lodge of the ancient order of Eclampses Vitus, of Centreville, Indiana,” was put off with a joke.
e-clampus-vitus-the-complete-record.s: The searches listed for the Connersville letter, with searches for “Jackson Lodge” with Clampus and Centreville, and the Indiana State Library’s archives catalogue.
e-clampus-vitus-the-complete-record.alt: The House Journal, 1846–47: No. 242, an act to incorporate Jackson Lodge of the ancient order of Eclampses Vitus, of Centreville, Indiana
e-clampus-vitus-the-complete-record.cap: Journal of the House of Representatives of Indiana, 1846–47. Internet Archive.

e-clampus-vitus-the-complete-record.t: A register of 61 places where E Clampus Vitus is on record before 1905, each with its earliest surviving record: the “complete list” of early lodges that the order’s historians wished for in 1966. The nearest earlier effort we know is Shumate’s list of about thirty places.
e-clampus-vitus-the-complete-record.s: Then and Now (1966), which names about fourteen places; the Shumate list as given by the Julia C. Bulette chapter; ecvinc.org and chapter websites; Wikipedia and its references; HMDB.

e-clampus-vitus-the-complete-record.t: The earliest dated California notice of the order yet found: the San Joaquin Republican of Stockton, 14 April 1852, calling members of the E. C. V. to their hall. The dates usually given are September 1852, or an undated record of 1851.
e-clampus-vitus-the-complete-record.s: Then and Now (1966); Wikipedia, which cites the Daily Alta California of 3 September 1852; the Sacramento Union of 28 September 1852; ecvinc.org and chapter websites; web searches for the Stockton notice.

e-clampus-vitus-the-complete-record.t: The Wheeling Daily Intelligencer of 1 February 1867 called Ephraim Bee “the recognized American head” of the order, and Caleb Cushing “the man who brought the secrets of the order to this country.”
e-clampus-vitus-the-complete-record.s: Wikipedia’s Ephraim Bee article and its references; the West Virginia Archives page on Bee, which prints a different Intelligencer sketch of 1863; ecvinc.org; web searches for the phrase.
e-clampus-vitus-the-complete-record.card: Wheeling Daily Intelligencer|Wheeling, West Virginia|1 February 1867

how-kalamazoo-got-its-name.t: The unnamed “atlas of 1823” that first spelled the river “Kikalemazo” is, we believe, Carey & Lea’s American Atlas: its map of Michigan Territory, dated 1822 and reissued in the atlas of 1823, letters the river “Kikalemazo R.”
how-kalamazoo-got-its-name.s: The Kalamazoo Public Library’s pages; Wikipedia’s “Etymology of Kalamazoo” and its source, Gannett’s Origin of Certain Place Names (1905); local news sites; web searches linking Carey & Lea and “Kikalemazo”.
how-kalamazoo-got-its-name.alt: Detail of the 1822 Carey and Lea map of Michigan Territory: the river lettered Kikalemazo R.
how-kalamazoo-got-its-name.cap: Carey & Lea, map of Michigan Territory, 1822. MSU Libraries.

how-kalamazoo-got-its-name.t: The story that Titus Bronson was fined for stealing a cherry tree has no 19th-century source we can find. It is not in the Pioneer Collections of 1877, Durant’s county history of 1880 or the Compendium of 1906, though each tells of Bronson and the change of name.
how-kalamazoo-got-its-name.s: The three histories named; the Kalamazoo Public Library’s Bronson biography; the City of Kalamazoo’s page; Wikipedia; local news sites that repeat the story.
how-kalamazoo-got-its-name.alt: Durant’s history of 1880 on Bronson after the renaming: he felt that he had been deeply wronged
how-kalamazoo-got-its-name.cap: Durant, History of Kalamazoo County (1880). Internet Archive.

how-niles-got-its-name.t: The explanation of the name Niles, for Hezekiah Niles of the Baltimore Register, enters the county histories only in 1906, with Coolidge, seventy-seven years after the plat. The detailed history of 1880 gives no reason for the name.
how-niles-got-its-name.s: The Berrien County histories of 1880 and 1906; Wikipedia’s Niles article; the Niles History Center; web searches for when the explanation first appears in print.
how-niles-got-its-name.alt: Coolidge’s history of 1906: the village was designated by Obed Lacey as Niles after the name of the editor of the Niles Register
how-niles-got-its-name.cap: Coolidge, Twentieth Century History of Berrien County (1906), p. 142. Internet Archive.

the-week-dewey-lake-went-wild.t: The 1882 county history records a warning chalked in red on a peeled tree at the fork of the old road to “Dewey’s Lake”: “Turn to the left and go to the Devil.” No telling of the 1964 Dewey Lake Monster that we found mentions it.
the-week-dewey-lake-went-wild.s: Wikipedia’s Dewey Lake Monster article; Robert Atkinson’s survey of the 1964 papers (2017); Visit Southwest Michigan’s haunted-places list; the Observer’s lake-monster article; web searches for the red-chalk sign with Dewey Lake.
the-week-dewey-lake-went-wild.alt: History of Cass County, 1882, p. 356: the road forked, one branch leading to Dewey’s Lake; on a tree in red chalk, Turn to the left and go to the Devil
the-week-dewey-lake-went-wild.cap: History of Cass County, Michigan (1882), p. 356. Internet Archive.

the-week-dewey-lake-went-wild.t: The lake behind the monster’s name was named for a pioneer. The county history of 1882 says Henry Dewey settled in Silver Creek because the land around “the lake which bears his name” had so much to recommend it. No telling of the Dewey Lake Monster that we found says who Dewey was.
the-week-dewey-lake-went-wild.s: History of Cass County, Michigan (1882), p. 356; Wikipedia’s Dewey Lake Monster article; Robert Atkinson’s survey (2017); Silver Creek Township’s own history page; web searches for Henry Dewey with Dewey Lake and Silver Creek.

the-week-dewey-lake-went-wild.t: Read against the township plat, the warning pointed one way. Coming up the old track from Indian Lake to the south-east corner of Section 16, a traveler bore left, to the north-west, to reach Dewey’s Lake. The left-hand road, the one the warning sent “to the Devil,” was the road to Dewey’s Lake.
the-week-dewey-lake-went-wild.s: The 1882 history’s account of the fork (p. 356); the plat of Silver Creek Township of about 1928; every telling of the red-chalk sign and the Dewey Lake story we could find.
the-week-dewey-lake-went-wild.alt: Plat of Silver Creek Township: Dewey Lake across Sections 8 and 9, with Section 16 below it

the-week-dewey-lake-went-wild.t: The description the whole country repeated in 1964, about nine feet tall and some five hundred pounds, first went out on the United Press wire in the words of Mrs. John Utrup, the farm wife who said it had chased her into her house. Later tellings give it to the berry pickers alone.
the-week-dewey-lake-went-wild.s: The United Press story of 11 June 1964 as printed in the Isabella County Daily Times-News (p. 1); Robert Atkinson’s survey of the 1964 papers (2017), which credits the Browns; Wikipedia’s Dewey Lake Monster article; web searches for Utrup with the height and weight.
the-week-dewey-lake-went-wild.alt: Isabella County Daily Times-News, 11 June 1964: Mrs. John Utrup of nearby Dewey Lakes told sheriff’s deputies the beast chased her into her home; it was nine feet tall, she said, and weighed 500 pounds
the-week-dewey-lake-went-wild.cap: Isabella County Daily Times-News, 11 June 1964, p. 1 (United Press). Digital Michigan Newspapers.

the-week-dewey-lake-went-wild.t: Two months after Dewey Lake, the United Press tied a new scare straight back to it: “Now Sheridan Has Its Own ‘Monster,’” a lion in Montcalm County, first Sister Lakes and now this. And the wire repeated Dewey Lake’s own explanation for the silence: other people had seen it, but did not talk about it “for fear of ridicule.” No telling of the Dewey Lake Monster that we found mentions the Sheridan sequel.
the-week-dewey-lake-went-wild.s: Isabella County Daily Times-News, 10 August 1964, p. 2 (United Press); Robert Atkinson’s survey (2017); Wikipedia; Notebook of Ghosts (2020); web searches for Sheridan, lion and Sister Lakes.

e-clampus-vitus-in-cassopolis-1846.t: The lodge of the “Ancient and Honorable Order of Eclampsus Vitus” instituted at Cassopolis in the spring of 1846, recorded by Rogers (1875) and Mathews (1882) with its four charter members named, is the earliest lodge of the order yet found anywhere with its members’ names written down, and the first known in Michigan.
e-clampus-vitus-in-cassopolis-1846.s: Full-text searches for “Eclampsus Vitus”, “Eclampses Vitus” and “Clampus Vitus”; Wikipedia’s articles on E Clampus Vitus and Ephraim Bee and their references; ecvinc.org and chapter websites; Then and Now (E Clampus Vitus, 1966); the Shumate list of early lodges; Rogers (1875) and Mathews (1882); the Cope genealogy of the Sharpless family (1887); Michigan newspapers of 1898.

e-clampus-vitus-in-cassopolis-1846.t: Three of the Cassopolis lodge’s four charter members married sisters of one family, the Bealls: a Niles obituary of September 1898 lists two of them as survivors of Nathaniel Beall, and the third married the youngest sister in 1854. The lodge was very nearly a family affair.
e-clampus-vitus-in-cassopolis-1846.s: Full-text searches for “Eclampsus Vitus”, “Eclampses Vitus” and “Clampus Vitus”; Wikipedia’s articles on E Clampus Vitus and Ephraim Bee and their references; ecvinc.org and chapter websites; Then and Now (E Clampus Vitus, 1966); the Shumate list of early lodges; Rogers (1875) and Mathews (1882); the Cope genealogy of the Sharpless family (1887); Michigan newspapers of 1898.

e-clampus-vitus-in-cassopolis-1846.t: The Cassopolis founders’ family came from Centreville, Indiana, the very town whose “Jackson Lodge” of the order asked the Indiana legislature for a charter that winter: the Beall sisters were born there, and the lodge’s young doctor read medicine there under a physician married to the sisters’ aunt.
e-clampus-vitus-in-cassopolis-1846.s: Full-text searches for “Eclampsus Vitus”, “Eclampses Vitus” and “Clampus Vitus”; Wikipedia’s articles on E Clampus Vitus and Ephraim Bee and their references; ecvinc.org and chapter websites; Then and Now (E Clampus Vitus, 1966); the Shumate list of early lodges; Rogers (1875) and Mathews (1882); the Cope genealogy of the Sharpless family (1887); Michigan newspapers of 1898.

the-indian-lake-sea-serpent.t: The state’s own fishery record shows what had just been put into Indian Lake before the 1898 serpent scare: five thousand lake trout fry in 1878, then four hundred thousand walleye fry in 1893 and again in 1897, the year before the serpent. The first survey, in 1887, found no muskellunge, and none was ever stocked. No telling of the Indian Lake serpent that we found mentions the stocking.
the-indian-lake-sea-serpent.s: The Michigan DNR’s Indian Lake Status of the Fishery Resource Report (2015-199); the 1898 and 1899 newspaper items; modern tellings of the serpent online; web searches for Indian Lake, serpent and stocking.
